# Lusa v1.1.0 - struct literals, zero-cost match, and compile-time modules

## Impact Introduction

v1.1.0 removes three sources of friction that appeared as Lusa programs grew.
Structs were useful for fixed layouts, but they had no literal syntax and every
field had to be assigned after declaration. Branching on a value required a
hand-written `if`/`elseif` chain, with no single place for the scrutinee and no
per-arm ownership story. Multi-file projects had no compile-time composition:
sharing a struct or helper meant copying source text or building a runtime
package.

This release closes those gaps. Struct declarations now accept brace and bare
forms, struct literals fill missing fields with deterministic defaults, and
nested struct/string/table fields get generated deep-drop and deep-clone
helpers. `match` evaluates its value once and lowers to an ordinary conditional
chain in every engine, with ownership checked separately per arm and no runtime
dispatcher. `import` and `mod` compose projects before parsing, recursively and
without duplicate definitions, while keeping one shared symbol table. Inline
assembly now uses the standard GNU volatile statement form behind a portable
macro.

The changes are implemented in the Rust front end and the self-hosted
`lexer.lusa`/`parser.lusa`/`compiler_bootstrap.lusa` pipeline, so the
interpreter, bytecode VM, `--emit-c`, and native builds agree on the same
programs.

## Feature Highlights

- **Two struct declaration forms** - `struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }` and
  `struct Point x: i32, y: i32 end` declare the same native layout.
- **Struct literals with defaults** - `Point{x: 10}` initializes `y` to `0`;
  omitted scalar fields become zero/`false`, omitted heap fields become `nil`.
- **Nested struct and heap fields** - fields may be scalars, `string`,
  `table`/`table<T>`, raw pointers, or previously declared structs. Native C
  embeds nested structs by value and uses declaration-order fields.
- **Deep struct RAII** - each declaration emits `lusa_drop_<Name>` and
  `lusa_clone_<Name>` helpers that recurse through nested struct, string, and
  table fields. Moves are tracked in the emitter's static move table.
- **Consistent struct value semantics** - scalar-only structs (including nested
  scalar-only structs) are Copy in the interpreter and VM; structs that own
  heap fields move like tables. Cloned structs keep their identity tags, so
  nested field reads do not accidentally move a value.
- **Zero-overhead `match`** - literal arms lower to `==` branches, a binding
  arm moves the value into a local, and `_` is the wildcard. Both parsers emit
  a hidden local plus an `if`/`elseif` chain; there is no match bytecode
  instruction and no C runtime arm table.
- **Per-arm ownership checking** - each arm is checked as its own scope, so a
  move in one arm cannot leak into another. Violations report the usual
  `E1001`/`E1002` diagnostics before code generation.
- **Compile-time modules** - `import "path.lusa"` and `mod name` expand
  recursively, resolve relative to the importing file, and deduplicate by
  canonical path. `mod a.b` finds `a/b.lusa`, `a/b/mod.lusa`, or
  `a/b/main.lusa`.
- **GNU-style inline assembly** - `unsafe_asm("wfe")` emits `LUSA_ASM("wfe")`,
  defined as `({ __asm__ volatile (text : : ); })` on GCC/Clang and as a no-op
  on toolchains without inline assembly.
- **ABI description updated** - `Compiler.memory_layout()` now reports native
  struct typedefs and the emitted drop/clone helpers.
- **Parity tests** - `tests/module15.rs` exercises both struct forms, literals,
  defaults, nested deep clone, match arms and ownership failures, recursive
  imports/modules with deduplication, and the inline-assembly form across all
  three engines.

## How to Use

Declare structs in either form, build values with literals, and let `clone`
deep-copy the heap fields:

```lusa
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

struct Label
    origin: Point,
    text: string
end

local p = Point{x: 10}                 -- y defaults to 0
local tag = Label{origin: p, text: "corner"}
print(tag.origin.x, tag.origin.y, tag.text)   -- 10	0	corner

local copy = clone tag
copy.origin.y = 9
copy.text = "copy"
print(tag.origin.y, copy.origin.y, copy.text) -- 0	9	copy

match tag.origin.x with
| 0 => print("at origin")
| other => print("offset", other)
end
```

`match` compares literal patterns and binds with a name. Put the binding or
wildcard arm last:

```lusa
match status with
| 0 => print("idle")
| 1 => print("busy")
| _ => print("unknown")
end
```

Split a project into compile-time modules. With `geo/point.lusa` containing:

```lusa
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

function make_point(x: i32, y: i32): Point
    return Point{x: x, y: y}
end
```

`main.lusa` can compose it directly:

```lusa
import "geo/point.lusa"

local p = make_point(2, 3)
print(p.x, p.y)                        -- 2	3
```

`mod geo.point` would resolve the same file if it were named
`geo/point.lusa`, `geo/point/mod.lusa`, or `geo/point/main.lusa`.

Run the bundled struct/match example in every engine:

```sh
lusalang run examples/struct_match.lusa
lusalang run examples/struct_match.lusa --vm
lusalang run examples/struct_match.lusa --native
```

Inspect the generated C, including the struct typedefs and RAII helpers:

```sh
lusalang build examples/struct_match.lusa --emit-c
```

Use inline assembly inside `unsafe` when a compiler with GNU inline assembly is
available:

```lusa
unsafe do
    unsafe_nop()
    unsafe_asm("wfe")
end
```

## Compatibility / Limits

- `struct`, `match`, `with`, `import`, and `mod` are now reserved keywords.
  Programs using them as variable or function names must rename those
  bindings. Member positions still accept keywords, so `string.match(...)` and
  `value:match()` keep working.
- Struct fields are limited to scalars, `string`, `table`/`table<T>`, raw
  pointer types, and previously declared structs. Forward struct references
  are rejected; declare a nested struct before using it as a field type.
- The dynamic engines emulate structs with tables. Structs made only of scalar
  fields follow Copy semantics; structs that own `string`/`table` fields move
  like tables. Native builds use real C typedefs with no dynamic field lookup.
- `match` patterns support numbers, strings, booleans, `nil`, one binding name,
  and `_`. Destructuring, guards, and range patterns are not part of this
  release. A binding or wildcard arm must be last.
- Imports are flat textual includes with one shared symbol table. There are no
  namespaces, export lists, or version resolution. Imported structs must appear
  before the literals or field types that use them.
- `unsafe_asm` accepts one plain string literal without quotes, backslashes, or
  newlines. GCC/Clang emit the requested instruction; other toolchains compile
  the no-op definition. Use only on targets where the instruction is valid.
- The native C11 backend remains a typed subset. Numeric `for`, varargs,
  interpolated strings, closures/nested functions, dynamic index assignment,
  and multiple function return values are still unsupported; the interpreter
  and `--vm` remain the complete-language engines.
- Exact `i128` arithmetic remains a native-backend feature; dynamic engines
  keep numbers as `f64`.

## Validation

The full suite passes with `cargo test --all-targets -- --test-threads=1`.
`tests/module15.rs` adds seven integration tests covering:

- both struct declaration syntaxes, literals, defaults, field access, and
  nested deep clone/drop;
- scalar-only struct copy semantics through nested fields and `clone` in the
  interpreter, VM, and native backend;
- emitted C typedefs, compound literals, and `lusa_drop_*`/`lusa_clone_*`
  helpers with no hash lookups for struct fields;
- literal, binding, and wildcard `match` arms with output parity and no runtime
  dispatcher;
- static and dynamic `E1001` failures for moves inside an arm;
- recursive imports and modules, relative paths, missing-file diagnostics, and
  one-inclusion deduplication;
- the GNU volatile inline-assembly form.

## Installation

Download `lusa-setup.zip` from the release assets, unzip it, and run
`install-lusa.cmd`. Platform tarballs contain the same standalone binary.
Building from source requires only `cargo build --release`; running Lusa
programs never requires cargo or Rust.
